first_impression: Solo 16-year-old compiling a Metal kernel for RL on a Mac? Real engineering, and the deck looks unusually polished.
confusing: Slide 9 compares a 2D impulse solver to MuJoCo HalfCheetah, so the 66x headline is not apples to apples
Slide 8 tripod 1.32 m/s next to slide 6 tripod reaching 7.2 m average reads inconsistent
Slide 11 headline 8,100 lines says nothing about quality or how much was generated
doubts: 8,100 lines and a compiler, PPO and CoreML export, all in 12 hours solo
CoreML 3.6e-7 error: which policy, which inputs
Walker replay at 1:00 shows 21.5 m in 8 s, yet the title counter reads 11.6 m
questions: How does the generated Metal kernel handle contact between bodies, one thread per robot with no inter-thread sync?
Is the PPO loop your own or a modified MLX example, and what is the 303K end-to-end number measured on?
Did you check that a policy trained in MacGym transfers to MuJoCo?

fixes.change: Put the honest caveat on the slide in larger type and add one MuJoCo-on-same-task bar (cartpole vs MuJoCo cartpole) so the comparison is like for like.
Show 3 lines of the generated Metal kernel source for the 15-line robot beside the pipeline.
Replace the line count with a git log screenshot or timeline of the day's milestones.
Add a 20-second live or recorded screen capture of the Playground training in the deck.

first_impression: Beautiful slides, but where is the demo? Fourteen slides of claims and no live proof. Show me it running.
confusing: Slides 2, 3 and 12 spend a lot of time on setup and audience before any live proof
Dot-morph animation is pretty but the 4,096 grid on slide 4 only shows 35 robots
Slide 13 roadmap is vapor: iPhone driving a real SO-101 arm is not built
doubts: 3.2 days of experience in 43 s: that is 4,096 envs times steps, is it real wall time with PPO included
Slide 7 data is one cherry-picked run
questions: Can you run the playground right now and show me the 4,096 tripods training?
How many seeds did you run, and does it learn every time?
What is the actual policy reward curve?

fixes.change: Cut slide 12 and slide 11, and replace with an embedded live demo or a screen recording of the browser Playground with the live training view.
Add a reward-vs-time curve across several seeds so it is clearly not one lucky run.
Shorten the roadmap to one line or drop it; spend the time on proof.
Say plainly that 3.2 days = 4,096 envs x sim time and show the formula in small type.

first_impression: Wow, a kid made a Metal GPU robot-learning framework alone in a day. The 'ordinary laptop' framing nails the theme.
confusing: Slide 5 is a little abstract: four dot icons do not show what the kernel really is
doubts: Speed comparison caveats are acknowledged, which I respect, but I want to see the sim is still physically sane
questions: What was the hardest bug today?
How much was written with AI help?
Which part are you proudest of?

fixes.change: Tie the build story to the theme: show the 11:38 AM commit and the hour-by-hour progress, to make the solo effort tangible.
Replace the abstract dot icons with the real code on the left and the real kernel on the right.
Add one real error screenshot of an NVIDIA-only simulator failing on a Mac, for a punchier problem.
Trim the roadmap so the closing line lands right after the proof.

first_impression: Looks gorgeous and clean. I get it fast: a robot that teaches itself to run on your laptop.
confusing: Slide 9 three bars all look the same height, so the chart says little
Slide 10 code is too small and dense to read from the back of the room
doubts: Is the robot actually learning or is it a pre-recorded animation
Is 'ordinary' really elevated here, it is a developer tool
questions: Can a regular student use this without knowing RL?
Can I see it learn right now?
What would I make with it?
